newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-China grain needs awesome, stays an importer.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-China grain needs awesome, stays an importer.

text.p: China will become the lion of the feed (coarse) grain market in the coming decade, importing ever larger amounts and eventually holding 18 percent of global trade, U.S. Feed Grains Council predicted Tuesday.
The council's forecast pegged Chinese feed grain imports of 4.2 million tonnes in 1997/98, zooming to 23.5 million tonnes in 2005/06, an average annual growth of 36 percent.
"The China numbers in the past few years have been frightening," said council analyst Erick Erickson, referring the abrupt switch from large exports to hefty imports.
"The turnaround is so big," Erickson said.
J.B. Penn, senior vice president of Sparks Companies Inc, which helped prepare the annual forecast, said that despite recent export sales of corn, China would be a net importer for the coming decade.
"China is not going to be a major feed grain exporter over the next 10 years," Penn told reporters.

Only three years ago, China exported more than 10 million tonnes of feed grains. According to USDA estimates, Beijing will import 2.2 million tonnes of feed grains this marketing year and export 500,000 tonnes.

Penn said the emerging middle class in China, numbering about 300 million now, would double in the next decade and its per capita income would double as well. The result would be huge demand for meats, dairy products and higher quality food.
"We are persuaded the potential is enormous. The demand is there," Penn said, particularly if the Chinese government sticks to goals of industrialization and low food prices.

The council's forecast suggested imports by China on the mammoth scale suggested last year by Lester Brown of the WorldWatch think tank. His projections have been under dispute because of large Chinese crops this year and minimal imports.
While the council did not agree with Brown's assumptions, Erickson said it reached a similar conclusion to Brown's provokative question: "Can China feed itself? No."

Feed Grains Council and USDA agreed on likely net imports by China this marketing year but differed on several points. USDA showed larger production and usage, by 10 million tonnes, than the council's 124 million tonnes and had a much larger supply based on 31 million tonnes of beginning stocks. The council did not estimate starting or ending stocks.
The council forecast was the first of several keynote global estimates to be released this year.
USDA will unveil its long-term baseline for U.S. and global crops at its Outlook Forum in late February.
"I think the council's nubmers are probably squarely in the middle of the pack," Erickson said. "We are not by any means standing alone in the field."

Penn said voracious demand by China for feed grain imports was one of three factors in a bullish outlook for feed grains. The others were healthy economic growth worldwide and less government interference in agriculture.
"China is the key to this," Penn said.
Erickson said U.S. share of the feed grain trade, now about 62 percent, would grow to 65-68 percent in the coming decade.
"I think we're going to do at least that well" in U.S. market share in China," Erickson said.
